title: Continuation Patterns
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/0/bod: After a **sharp, strong** move (the flagpole), price takes a short break and drifts a little lower between **two parallel lines** (the flag). A break above the flag usually means **the earlier move continues**.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/1/bod: The difference from a flag: the pause after the pole forms a **small triangle** with converging lines instead of two parallel lines. The logic is the same: after the break, the earlier move is more likely to continue.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/2/exp: A sharp drop (the pole), then a small upward correction between two parallel lines: a bear flag. A break below the flag usually means the drop continues.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/3/pro: Tap the candle that broke out of the flag to the upside.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/3/exp: This is the first candle that closed above the flag's upper line. The break was over and the move up continued.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/4/sta: In a bull flag, the flag itself usually slopes slightly down or moves sideways.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/4/exp: The flag is a short correction against the pole. In a bull flag, price drifts a little lower or sideways, then carries on.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/5/bod: A common way to set the target: measure the **pole's length** from the **flag's breakout point**. Volume is usually **high** on the pole, **drops** during the flag, and **picks up** again on the breakout.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/6/pro: On Bitcoin, the flagpole ran from 58,000 to 62,000 and the flag broke upward at 61,500. Where's the rough target?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/6/exp: Pole length = 62,000 − 58,000 = 4,000. From the breakout point: 61,500 + 4,000 = 65,500. It's a rough target, and price may turn back sooner.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/7/pro: After a sharp drop, Ethereum formed a bear flag and the last candle closed below the flag. What do you do?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/7/exp: A strong bearish pole, an upward-sloping flag, and now a break below the flag: a further drop is more likely. The logical stop loss is above the flag's high.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/8/pai: A small correction between two parallel lines
Price exiting in the pole's direction
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/9/pro: What does volume usually look like in a classic bull flag?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/9/opt: High on the pole, low in the flag, high again on the breakout
Roughly constant from start to finish
Low on the pole and very high in the flag
High only while the flag is forming
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l1/steps/9/exp: The pole forms with excitement and high volume, the market rests in the flag and volume dries up, and a real breakout usually comes with high volume again.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/0/bod: In a **symmetrical triangle**, the highs get **lower** and the lows get **higher**, so the two lines converge: the market is **coiling up**. It's usually treated as a **continuation** pattern, but you still have to see which way it breaks.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/1/bod: In an **ascending triangle**, the highs sit at roughly **the same level** and the lows keep **rising**. Buyers are pushing, and many traders see an upside break as more likely. A **descending triangle** is the reverse: a flat floor and lower highs.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/2/pro: What kind of triangle is this?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/2/exp: The lows are roughly flat at 2380 and the highs keep getting lower: a descending triangle. Sellers are pushing.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/3/pro: Tap the candle that broke the ascending triangle to the upside.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/3/exp: This is the first candle that closed above the flat 3100 resistance. Buyers finally broke the ceiling.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/4/sta: In an ascending triangle, the lows are roughly level and the highs keep getting lower.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/4/exp: That describes a descending triangle. In an ascending triangle the upper line is flat (resistance) and the lows keep rising: buyers step in earlier each time.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/5/bod: A common triangle target: the **height of the widest part**, measured from the **breakout point**. Breakouts usually happen before price reaches the **apex**; the closer price gets to the apex, the weaker the breakout tends to be.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/5/tip: Until a candle closes outside the triangle, don't guess the breakout direction.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/6/pro: You have a symmetrical triangle on gold: its widest part ran from 2380 to 2440, and price broke upward at 2420. Where's the rough target?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/7/pro: GBP/USD was in a descending triangle and the last candle closed below the flat 1.2600 floor. What do you do?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/7/exp: The descending triangle's flat floor broke, and the lower highs had already shown sellers were stronger. A further drop is more likely; stop loss above the triangle's last high.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/8/sen: The ___ triangle has a flat upper line and rising lows, while the ___ triangle has a flat lower line and falling highs.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/8/exp: An ascending triangle has flat resistance and higher lows; a descending triangle has flat support and lower highs.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/9/pro: A symmetrical triangle formed in the middle of an uptrend. Which read is more accurate?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/9/opt: An upside break is more likely, but wait for a close outside the triangle
It will definitely break up; buy right now
A symmetrical triangle is always bearish
Breakout direction doesn't matter; only volume does
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l2/steps/9/exp: A symmetrical triangle usually continues the prior trend, but that's a probability, not a rule. Entering after a close outside the triangle protects you from lots of fake breakouts.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/0/bod: After a trend, price bounces between a **flat ceiling** and a **flat floor**, just like a range. Many traders treat the rectangle as a **continuation** pattern and expect the breakout to go **in the direction of the prior trend**.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/1/bod: Option one: trade **inside the rectangle**, buying near the floor and selling near the ceiling (with stops outside the rectangle). Option two: wait for a **breakout on a close** outside the rectangle. The usual breakout target is the **rectangle's height** from the breakout point.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/2/pro: What pattern is this, and which way do many traders expect it to break?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/2/opt: Inverse head and shoulders; bullish reversal
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/2/exp: After a drop, price ranged between 60,000 and 61,500: a rectangle. Since the prior trend was down, many expect a downside break. But until the real breakout, nothing is certain.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/3/pro: Tap the candle that broke out of the rectangle to the upside.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/3/exp: This is the first candle that closed above the rectangle's top (2415). The candles before it only touched the top and turned back.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/4/pro: EUR/USD formed a rectangle between 1.0850 and 1.0900 and has now closed above 1.0900. Where's the rough target?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/4/exp: Rectangle height = 50 pips. From the breakout point: 1.0900 + 0.0050 = 1.0950.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/5/sta: Inside a rectangle, before the breakout, buying near support and selling near resistance is also a common approach.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/5/exp: As long as the rectangle holds, its edges act as support and resistance. Just keep your stop outside the rectangle, because one day it will break.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/6/tit: A valid breakout: volume and pullback
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/6/bod: A rectangle breakout is more reliable when the breakout candle has a **strong body** and **high volume**. Afterwards, price often comes back to test **the old ceiling as support**, and many traders use that pullback to enter.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/7/pro: Ethereum broke up out of the 3000 to 3060 rectangle on high volume, and on the pullback to 3060 it printed a green candle. What do you do?
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/7/exp: The breakout came on high volume, and the rectangle's old top has now acted as support. A continuation up is more likely; stop loss below the pullback low, inside the rectangle.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/8/pro: Put the steps of trading a rectangle breakout in order.
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/8/ite: Draw the rectangle's top and bottom
Wait for a candle to close outside the rectangle
Enter and put your stop inside the rectangle
lessons/chart-patterns-u2-l3/steps/8/exp: Without the prior trend, you don't know which break is more likely. Then draw the range, wait for a close outside it, and finally enter with a clear stop loss.
